Build a dark editorial landing whose hero is a preference→product relationship graph.

**Palette:** `#0B0B0F` canvas, `#15151B` panel surface, `#6E56CF` as the single brand violet (CTA, active node, highlighted edges, one accent word in the headline), `#a894f7` for node icons and strength bars, `#A1A1AA` for secondary text, white for headline and figures.

**Type:** extra-bold headline at `clamp(2.2rem,7.4vw,3rem)` → `lg:clamp(3rem,4.6vw,4.4rem)`, leading 1.0, tracking -0.02em; body at 1.6 leading; a 7rem ghost numeral at `white/[0.04]`; `tabular-nums` + 0.12em tracking on every match figure.

**Hero:** a left rail of five preference signals (Style, Size, Budget, Condition, Trend) as a vertical roving `role="tablist"`, a right column of four product cards, and between them an SVG in a `0 0 100 100` viewBox drawing twenty edges. Edge opacity and stroke-width come from a real strength table.

**The rule that matters:** selecting a signal must recompute *at least* four things simultaneously — the evidence panel heading, the reasoning sentence, all four comparative strength bars, and which product card is highlighted. A hero where one click moves one number is a hero that reads as static.

**Accessibility & motion:** tabs carry `aria-selected` and `aria-controls` pointing at the evidence panel; arrow keys move the roving focus; `pathLength` edge animation is disabled under `prefers-reduced-motion`.

**Images:** product-card badges (match %, grade, verification, discount) sit in a scrim at the base of the photo, never overlaid on the image itself.

palette.usage: Screen background and every row card's fill, plus the alert switch's off-state track — an unset switch reads as empty rather than as a gray chip

palette.role: Accent — spent on the drop event only
palette.usage: The filled 'Down' badge on rows whose price fell, the sparkline stroke, and the switch track when a price alert is armed. Nothing else on this screen is allowed to take it
The drop badge's numeral and the switch thumb when the alert is on
The 'Watchlist' heading and the current price, the only two things on the screen at full contrast
Item titles, and the label of a rise badge (an increase is stated in ink, never in a warning hue)
The percentage printed next to each sparkline, so the number reads as a caption to the line rather than competing with the price
The '5 saved items / 3 price drops' subline, the struck-through original price, the 'Price alert' caption, the no-change badge label, and the off-state switch thumb
Row card hairlines, the outlined badge used for rises and no-change, and the outline of an off-state switch track

n1.typography: System face with numeric weight steps rather than families. Heading 28/800 with -0.5 letter spacing; subline 13 in faint. Inside a row the hierarchy is carried by three sizes on one baseline: current price 17/800 with tabular-nums, original price 13 struck through, title 15/600 at 21 line-height clipped to one line. The trend percentage is 12/600 tabular so the sign column never shifts as values change, and the badge label is 12/700 tabular. The 'Price alert' caption drops to 11 — the smallest type on the screen sits under the only control on it.
n1.spacing: 4/8 rhythm from tokens.space(n). Horizontal padding space(5) = 20 with a deep space(14) = 56 top inset that lets the heading breathe without a nav bar. The list adds space(5) vertical padding and space(3) = 12 between rows; each card is padded space(4) = 16 with a space(3) gutter between the info block and the alert column. Inside the info block the rhythm tightens to raw pixels rather than tokens — 8 above the price row, 10 above the badge, 6 between switch and caption — because these are optical adjustments within one card, not layout structure. The sparkline is a fixed 60x22 pushed right with margin-auto so every row's trend graphic lands on the same axis regardless of price length.
n1.philosophy: Watchlist answers one question per row without opening anything: how far has this moved since I saved it. That forces three facts onto a single line — the current price, the original struck through, and a 12-point sparkline with its percentage printed beside it — rather than deferring them to a detail tap. The silhouette is deliberately horizontal: the title block sits outside the FlatList so the count line stays put while rows scroll, and each card runs left-to-right, an info block against an alert column, which separates it at a glance from MatchList's vertical stack. The single accent is spent on exactly one event, a filled badge for a price drop; rises and flat rows get an outlined badge and carry direction in the sign of the number, never in a hue, because a one-accent palette has no red/green pair to spend and should not invent one. The switch is built from the two token radii alone — radius.md on a 24-tall track makes a pill, radius.sm on a 12px thumb makes a circle — so a control that every screen reuses introduces no screen-local geometry.

dosDonts.do: Print the trend percentage next to the sparkline and give the sparkline an accessibility label that states the item, the window, and the change.
dosDonts.dont: Ship a bare line and expect the shape to carry the value — a 60x22 graphic has no resolution to be read numerically, and none at all to a screen reader.

dosDonts.do: Spend the single accent on the drop badge only, and let rises and flat rows use the outlined variant.
dosDonts.dont: Add a second hue for rises. A near-monochrome palette cannot afford a red/green pair, and direction is already carried by the sign.

dosDonts.do: Keep the original price visible and struck through beside the current one.
dosDonts.dont: Replace the original with a percentage alone — the comparison is the reason the row exists, and the reader wants both anchors.

dosDonts.do: Build the alert switch from radius.md (track) and radius.sm (thumb) so it reads as pill plus circle using only token values.
dosDonts.dont: Hard-code a 999 pill radius for one control — it becomes the exception every later screen copies.

dosDonts.do: Give the switch accessibilityRole 'switch' with a checked state and a label naming the item.
dosDonts.dont: Leave it as a plain pressable View — an unlabeled toggle in a list of five is indistinguishable to a screen reader.

# Recreate: Watchlist (saved items with price alerts)

Build a React Native list screen for saved secondhand items, where every row answers 'how far has this moved since I saved it' without a tap.

**Palette:** white canvas and white cards; a single indigo accent (#4f46e5) reserved for exactly three things — the filled price-drop badge, the sparkline stroke, and an armed alert switch. Ink #18181b for the heading and the current price, #27272a for titles, #52525b for the trend percentage, #71717a for the struck-through original price and captions, #e4e4e7 for card hairlines and outlined badges. No second hue: rises and no-change use an outlined badge and state direction with the sign of the number.

**Type:** heading 28/800 at -0.5 tracking; title 15/600; current price 17/800 tabular-nums; original price 13 struck through; trend percentage 12/600 tabular; captions 11.

**Layout:** the heading and the '5 saved items / 3 price drops' subline sit outside the list so they stay put while rows scroll. Each row is horizontal — an info block (title, then a baseline-aligned price row of current + original + a right-pushed 60x22 sparkline with its percentage, then a badge) against a narrow right column holding the switch and its caption. Cards are 1px bordered, radius 12, padded 16, gapped 12. Screen padding 20 with a 56 top inset. No fixed bottom bar.

**Behavior:** the switch is local state seeded from fixed data; the sparkline is static and deterministic (min/max normalized, fixed 12-point series, no random or clock APIs). Prices are formatted by hand rather than toLocaleString so output is environment-independent.

**Accessibility:** switch role with a checked state and a label naming the item; the sparkline is one image-role container carrying item, window and change in its label, with its internals not individually announced.

**Feel:** three numbers on one line, one accent spent on one event, and nothing hidden behind a tap.

The filled grade chip (S/A/B) in each card head and the fill of every match-factor bar; the chip and the bars are the only accent on the screen
The single grade letter inside the chip, kept at 700 weight so one character survives on a small filled shape
The 'AI Match Results' heading and the 0-100 match score, the number the card is built around
Item titles at two lines, and the numeral printed at the end of every factor bar
The price line under the title and the factor names (Condition, Price, Rarity, Demand) in the left column of the bar rows
The 'picks today' subline and the uppercase 'MATCH FACTORS' caption that opens the breakdown
Card hairlines, and the unfilled track behind every factor bar — the same neutral does container duty and scale duty, so a bar reads as a proportion of a visible whole

n2.typography: Heading 28/800 at -0.5 tracking over a 13 faint subline. Inside the card the score is 20/800 with tabular-nums so four cards' scores align optically down the list, and the grade chip is 12/700 on accent. Title 15/600 at 21 line-height, clamped to two lines; price 14 muted tabular. The breakdown opens with an 11/700 uppercase caption at 0.4 tracking — the same label treatment used for section captions across the native set — and each bar row is a fixed 52px factor name at 12, a 120px bar, and a 26px right-aligned 12/700 tabular value.
n2.spacing: 4/8 rhythm. Screen padding space(5) = 20, top inset space(14) = 56, list gap space(3) = 12 with 20 of vertical padding. Cards are padded space(4) = 16 at radius 12. Within a card the vertical rhythm is a deliberate ramp of raw offsets rather than tokens: 12 above the title, 6 above the price, 14 above the factor caption, 12 above the bars, 6 between bars. The ramp widens exactly where the card changes register — from identity (grade, score, title, price) to evidence (the breakdown) — so the two halves separate without a divider rule.
n2.philosophy: AI Match Results argues that a score is worthless unless the card also shows what produced it. Each card puts a grade chip and a 0-100 score in tension across one head row, then spends its lower half breaking that score into four factor bars whose values are always printed, never hovered for — the bars are sorted descending on render, so the reason a match ranked where it did is the first thing read after the score. The encoding is one accent on a neutral track: the bar fill is the accent, the track is the same hairline used for card borders, and no factor gets a hue of its own, which keeps four bars comparable rather than categorical. The silhouette matches Watchlist deliberately — a fixed title block above a single FlatList, no bottom band — because both are browse screens with nothing to complete; the difference is the card, which stacks vertically here against Watchlist's horizontal row, so the two lists are distinguishable at a glance even though they share every token.

dosDonts.do: Print each factor's value at the end of its bar and sort the bars descending on every render.
dosDonts.dont: Let bar length alone carry the value, or preserve the source array's order — an unsorted breakdown makes four cards uncomparable.

dosDonts.do: Draw the bar track in the same hairline neutral used for card borders, and fill it with the single accent.
dosDonts.dont: Give each factor its own color. Four hues turn a comparison into a legend the reader has to learn.

dosDonts.do: Put grade and score on one head row, at opposite ends, so the card opens with its two summary facts.
dosDonts.dont: Stack grade above score — it doubles the card's vertical cost and hides the number the list is ranked by.

dosDonts.do: Collapse the whole breakdown into one image-role container whose label reads every factor and value as a sentence.
dosDonts.dont: Leave a dozen SVG rects individually focusable — the chart becomes an obstacle course in a screen reader.

dosDonts.do: Keep the vertical card stack when the sibling list already uses a horizontal row.
dosDonts.dont: Reuse the same card silhouette across two lists that share a palette — with one accent and one neutral ramp, layout is the only thing left to tell them apart.

# Recreate: AI Match Results (scored recommendation list)

Build a React Native list of secondhand items an AI has scored, where each card proves its own score.

**Palette:** white canvas and white cards separated by #e4e4e7 hairlines. One indigo accent (#4f46e5) used twice only — the filled grade chip and the factor-bar fill. Ink #18181b for the heading and the score, #27272a for titles and bar values, #52525b for price and factor names, #71717a for the subline and the uppercase caption. The bar track is the same #e4e4e7 as the card border, so a bar reads as a share of a visible whole.

**Type:** heading 28/800 at -0.5; score 20/800 tabular-nums; grade chip 12/700 on accent; title 15/600 clamped to two lines; price 14 muted tabular; an 11/700 uppercase 0.4-tracked 'MATCH FACTORS' caption; bar rows of a 52px name at 12, a 120px bar, and a 26px right-aligned 12/700 tabular value.

**Layout:** a fixed title block (heading + 'N picks today') above a single scrolling list; no bottom bar. Cards are vertical stacks: head row with grade left and score right, then title, price, caption, and four horizontal bars. Screen padding 20, 56 top inset, 12 between cards, 16 card padding, radius 12. Widen the internal rhythm where the card turns from identity to evidence instead of adding a divider.

**Behavior:** bars sort descending by value on render and always print the numeral; data is fixed and deterministic, with factor values averaging to roughly the score. Nothing animates.

**Accessibility:** one image-role container per breakdown, labeled with every factor and value as a sentence; the card is a button labeled with title and score.

**Feel:** the score is the headline and the bars are the argument, both readable in one pass.

palette.usage: Screen background and the fill of the single chart card, so the plot area is the same white as the page and only the hairline marks its edge
The 2px price line, the area beneath it at 14 percent opacity, and the 3.5r dot on the active point. The series is the only thing on this screen holding the accent
The 'Price History' heading, the current price at 24/800, and the fill of the tooltip bubble — the one place ink is used as a surface rather than as text
The value inside the tooltip bubble at 12/700, white on ink so the number stays legible over the plotted area
The product title under the heading, clamped to two lines
The signed change percentage sitting on the same baseline as the current price
The 'tap the chart' caption, the 10px axis tick labels on both axes, the dashed crosshair, and the day label inside the tooltip bubble
The chart card's hairline and the three horizontal gridlines at max, midpoint and min — grid and container share one neutral so the plot never gains a second structural tone

n3.typography: Heading 28/800 at -0.5 tracking; product title 15/600 at 21 line-height. The current price steps up to 24/800 with tabular-nums and shares a baseline with a 14/700 signed percentage, so the headline reads as one phrase rather than two blocks. The caption under it is 12 faint. Inside the chart everything drops to SVG text at 10 for axis ticks, and the tooltip is a two-line block: day at 10 faint above value at 12/700 white. Y ticks are compacted to a rounded thousands form (480000 becomes 480K) so a 46px left gutter is enough for the axis.
n3.spacing: 4/8 rhythm. Screen padding space(5) = 20 with a space(14) = 56 top inset, matching the browse screens so a push from a list does not shift the heading. Header offsets tighten downward — 10 above the title, 8 above the price row, 4 above the caption — then the chart card takes space(4) = 16 of separation and space(3) = 12 of internal padding. Inside the SVG the padding is asymmetric on purpose: 46 left for the value axis, 10 right, 12 top, 22 bottom for day labels. Chart width is computed as the window width minus both screen paddings, then clamped to 260-520; height is fixed at 200.
n3.philosophy: Price History is the only screen in the native set with no list at all — a static header block over a single chart card — and the chart is the entire argument. Its tooltip is a default, not a reveal: the active index initializes to the last point, so the crosshair, the dot and the value bubble are already drawn before anyone touches the screen, and a PanResponder only lets a finger scrub the series and snap to the nearest index. That is the same commitment the gallery's heatmap makes in a different medium — the value is printed before the interaction, and interaction only moves it. The width is clamped to 260-520 against the window rather than filling it, because a 14-point series stretched across a tablet flattens into a line that reads as no change at all. One accent carries the whole series in three intensities (stroke, 14 percent area, dot), gridlines borrow the card's own hairline, and the only dark surface on the screen is the tooltip bubble — inverting ink into a fill exactly once, where a number has to survive on top of the plot.

dosDonts.do: Initialize the tooltip to the latest point so the current value is on screen before any touch.
dosDonts.dont: Start with no active point and wait for a gesture — on a chart-only screen that leaves the primary number unstated.

dosDonts.do: Clamp chart width to a 260-520 range computed from the window.
dosDonts.dont: Let the plot fill any width — a short series stretched wide reads as a flat, meaningless line.

dosDonts.do: Keep the tooltip bubble inside the plot by clamping its x against both paddings and flipping it below the point when it would overflow the top.
dosDonts.dont: Anchor the bubble rigidly above the dot — at the series maximum it clips out of the SVG.

dosDonts.do: Draw gridlines in the same hairline neutral as the card border and label ticks in a compact thousands form.
dosDonts.dont: Introduce a separate grid tone or print full-width currency on the axis — the gutter doubles and the plot loses width.

dosDonts.do: Give the chart one image-role container whose label states the item, the start value, the current value and the change.
dosDonts.dont: Rely on the visible tooltip for the value — a scrub gesture is not available to every reader.

The payout in the action bar is 26/800 tabular-nums, an offer card's amount 22/800, the stepper's counter amount 22/800, the pinned amount 20/800; all tabular, so stepping by ten thousand never shifts the layout. Message text is the only 16/22 body on the screen, which is what makes the conversation read as conversation next to the structured cards. dosDonts.dont: Distinguish live from expired by border color alone — with one accent there is no second state color to spend.

dosDonts.do: Require choose-then-confirm for accept, decline and send, and keep a withdraw affordance on a sent counter.
dosDonts.dont: Commit money on a single tap, or settle into a state with no way back and no explanation of what happens next.

dosDonts.do: Always render the bound hint under the stepper, even when it is just the allowed range.
dosDonts.dont: Render it conditionally — the composer's height jumps under the reader's thumb as they step across a boundary.

dosDonts.do: Anchor the thread to its newest entry on content-size change only.
dosDonts.dont: Scroll to the end on every render or on a timer — it fights a reader who has scrolled back through the history.

Build a React Native negotiation screen as three bands: a header with a pinned live-offer strip, a time-ordered thread that takes the remaining height, and a persistent bottom action bar. You are the seller.

**Palette:** white canvas and white bands separated by hairlines (#e4e4e7). One indigo accent (#4f46e5) meaning 'this is the round in play' — live offer card border, Live pill fill, expiry progress fill, selected preset chip, the signed payout delta, and the primary commit button. Ink #18181b for every figure being decided; #27272a for secondary text and, as a fill, your own message bubbles and the strong confirm button used for declining; #52525b for captions and superseded amounts; #71717a for bylines, day rules and system events; #e4e4e7 as the fill of the counterparty's bubbles, which is what puts the two parties on opposite tonal sides.

Build a light, commercial link-analytics dashboard for marketers. The organising idea: this page answers "what should I fix today", so every metric is followed by an action and the actions are wired back into the charts.

**The prescription cards are the point.** Each holds a severity badge (critical / warning / opportunity, each with its own lucide icon and tone), a one-line title, an evidence sentence, a small bar chart with the offending bars highlighted, a primary Fix-this button, and a **Show on chart** toggle that drops a dashed vertical marker plus a square node into the hero time series at that finding's date and prints a caption strip beneath it. Cards can be queued, snoozed or dismissed into a dashed placeholder with an Undo, and a counter reports how many of three are handled.

**Palette.** `zinc-50` canvas, `white` cards with `zinc-200` hairlines, rounded-xl, shadow-sm. Split the orange accent by contrast need: `orange-700` for text, buttons and active carets, `orange-600` for fills only (brand tile, chart line and gradient, share bars, flow nodes). The peak multiple and the send-time ratio are computed and injected into the copy — never typed into the sentence.

**Palette.** `zinc-950` canvas, `zinc-900/60` cards, `rose-500` for the brand tile, primary button and low-alpha selection tints, `rose-400` as the single focus-ring colour. Status is a four-rung ladder — emerald on-time, amber at-risk, rose delayed, zinc delivered — always a dot plus an abbreviated word. ETA deltas carry a sign, an icon and a figure. Hold every muted line at `zinc-400`; nothing dimmer.

**Type.** Pretendard, with `--font-display-grotesk` in exactly two places: the wordmark and the hero on-time percentage. Exactly three weights: 400 / 500 / 600. 11px uppercase tracked labels; a fractional body ladder (13.5 / 13 / 11.5 / 11 / 10px) so a 320px rail row carries lane, carrier and delta without truncation. Everything numeric is tabular-nums, hours to one decimal.

**Determinism and edges.** Every value is a pure function of a fixed seed and every date label is offset arithmetic from a fixed anchor — no Math.random, no Date.now, no live date objects. Reset palette state by comparing to previous state during render, not by setting state inside an effect. Flip the carrier annotation to the left of its point past about 68% of the plot width, or it runs past the page edge at 390px. Give the Cmd-K trigger an accessible name that survives its label being hidden at narrow widths.

palette.usage: The landing's outermost ground. Everything else is a lift off this, never a tint of it — the dark here is near-black rather than a blue-grey, so the single violet accent reads as the only chromatic event on the page.
The inspector device, the four spec-sheet cards, the FAQ rows. Measured on eight elements — a single raised step, not a ladder of five greys, which is what keeps a dark page from turning muddy.

Headlines, card titles, verdict labels. Pure white rather than an off-white: on #0b0b0f the extra contrast buys headroom for the mono display face, which renders visually lighter than a grotesk at the same weight.

Findings copy, spec-sheet rows, FAQ answers — 59 text nodes, the most-used foreground on the page. 8.6:1 on the ground, which clears AA with room to spare and is the reason the page can carry this much prose without a second surface tone.
CTA pills, the active layer chip, the filled verdict badge, the confidence bar. Five painted elements on the whole page — the near-monochrome rule means the accent has to earn each appearance.

White, not dark ink. On #6e56cf white measures 5.39:1 and dark ink 3.64:1, so body-size text on the fill needs white to clear AA. This work is the reason the canon says so — it shipped with dark ink at a11y 96 and the round's own gate caught it.

The idle layer chip's icon and label, where the accent must read as text rather than as a fill. Derived light rather than the accent itself: #6e56cf as small text on the ground is 3.73:1 and would fail, this tint is 9.1:1.
The few light-on-dark inversions — the photo caption plate and the pull-quote mark. Reserved for genuinely light grounds; it is never placed on the accent fill.

v12.typography: Two faces, one of which is a display: Pretendard Variable for body and Korean, and --font-display-mono (JetBrains Mono Display) for headlines, the verdict labels and every number in the inspector. The mono face is the argument — a page about machine inspection reads its findings in the face a machine would print them in, and it makes the confidence percentages align without tabular-nums doing the work alone. Exactly three weights render: 400 for prose, 600 for labels and chips, 700 for the headline. Scale measured at 1440: 38.4px headline, 18px section leads, 16px body, 14px card rows, 12px chips, 11.52px eyebrows and findings — the 11.52px step carries 46 nodes, so it is the page's real workhorse and is why the muted tone had to be #a1a1aa rather than anything dimmer.
v12.spacing: A 6/4/8 base rhythm rather than a strict 4 or 8 grid: 6px is the most-used gap (24 occurrences — chip rows, badge-to-label, rail segments), 4px binds icon to text, 8px separates card rows, 12px and 16px handle card interiors, and 32px/96px set section breathing. The hero is a 12-column asymmetric split rather than a centred stack, with the inspector device on the wide side and the findings column narrow beside it; below lg the two swap into a single column and the findings move after the product cards, because the first fold must keep the listing cards visible. Body measure is capped by ch, not px — max-w-[58ch] on editorial prose and FAQ answers, which measures 62–68 characters and sits under the 75-character ceiling the canon defines as the only failure direction.
v12.philosophy:
The proof is the resting state, and the interaction sharpens it rather than revealing it. On load the photo already carries a verdict badge, a confidence bar and a finding — nothing has to be clicked to learn what the AI concluded. Toggling one of the three inspection layers (condition, authenticity, price fairness) recomputes four surfaces at once: the badge label, the bar width and percentage, the highlighted region drawn over the photo, and the finding sentence. That is the difference between a control that discloses content and a control that changes an answer.

The page also settles an argument the loop had been having with itself for six rounds. Macro skeletons had been converging, so this round assigned each candidate a different one; this candidate drew the inspector hero, and the assignment worked — the skeletons genuinely diverged. What did not diverge was the closing CTA band, which came out identical across all three. The lesson recorded in the canon is that convergence moves down a level rather than disappearing, and that assignment should stop at the macro skeleton rather than chase it downward.

It won from a complete three-way draw. Lens 1 ranked it second, lens 2 third, lens 3 first; the tie-break rule excluded lens 1's leader because lens 3 had placed that candidate last, and the remainder resolved to this one. Second use of that rule.

dosDonts.do: Put white on the accent fill for any text at body size. Measure it: #ffffff on #6e56cf is 5.39:1, dark ink is 3.64:1.
dosDonts.dont: Follow the older instinct that a bright fill wants dark ink. It holds for ≥24px and for non-text, and fails everything else — this page shipped at a11y 96 for exactly that reason.

dosDonts.do: Show a verdict, a confidence value and a finding before any interaction happens.
dosDonts.dont: Hide the proof behind the toggle. A control that reveals content is a disclosure widget, not a demonstration.

dosDonts.do: Let one toggle move several surfaces — badge, bar, photo highlight and sentence together.
dosDonts.dont: Recompute a single number. One moving figure reads as a counter, not as a model changing its mind.

dosDonts.do: Keep the listing cards inside the first fold, moving the findings column below them on narrow screens.
dosDonts.dont: Push the product below the hero on mobile to protect the hero's composition. The canon puts product and proof in the first fold, and the hero is what yields.

dosDonts.do: Derive a lighter tint (#b6a6f0) when the accent has to act as small text.
dosDonts.dont: Use #6e56cf itself for small text on the dark ground — it measures 3.73:1 and fails.

dosDonts.do: Use the mono display face for findings and figures, where machine-printed is the point.
dosDonts.dont: Extend it to body prose. Two display faces in one work is a canon violation, and mono at paragraph length costs more reading speed than it buys in character.

dosDonts.do: Add contain:layout to a mobile-only horizontal scroller nested inside a grid.
dosDonts.dont: Assume the local overflow stays local — with three or more cards it leaks into document.documentElement.scrollWidth and the sweep gate fails at widths that look fine by eye.

v12.agentPrompt:
Build a dark landing page whose hero is an AI inspection device rather than a headline.

Ground #0b0b0f with a single raised surface #111116 — one step, not a ladder. White #ffffff for headlines, #a1a1aa for the prose that carries most of the page. One accent, #6e56cf, painted on no more than five elements; text sitting on that fill is white (5.39:1), never dark ink (3.64:1, fails AA at body size). When the accent must act as small text instead of a fill, derive #b6a6f0.

Two faces: Pretendard for body, one display face for headlines, verdict labels and every figure — a monospace display reads as machine-printed and suits an inspection subject. Exactly three weights: 400/600/700. Scale 38.4 / 18 / 16 / 14 / 12 / 11.52px, and expect the 11.52px step to carry the most nodes, which is why the muted tone cannot go dimmer than #a1a1aa.

The hero: one real product photo, three inspection layers as toggle chips (condition, authenticity, price fairness). On load the page already shows a verdict badge, a confidence bar with its percentage, a highlighted region on the photo and a finding sentence. Toggling a layer recomputes all four at once. Do not gate the proof behind the interaction.

Below the hero, four spec-sheet listing cards — and they must be inside the first fold at every width. On narrow screens move the findings column below the cards rather than pushing the cards down. If you use a mobile-only horizontal scroller for the cards, add contain:layout to it, or the local overflow will leak into the document's scrollWidth once there are three or more.

Then editorial long-form in three image/text blocks, an FAQ accordion, a single pull quote, a closing CTA. Cap prose by ch, not px — 58ch lands at 62–68 characters, under the 75-character ceiling.

No ghost numbers, no numbered sections, no three-column value split, no stat strip. Those skeletons are taken.

palette.usage: Pure white across all four wizard steps, measured on thirteen elements — the only surface tone in the screen. A creation flow that tints its steps to signal progress ends up teaching the tint instead of the task.
Step titles, field labels, the price figure. Near-black rather than pure black, which is the native DNA's choice and keeps long-form entry from vibrating against the white ground.

Field help, the suggested-price reference, review-step values. Nine nodes — the tier that carries the wizard's explanations, and the reason the muted tier below it had to stay above the dark-on-light floor.

Step counter, section captions, the placeholder state of unfilled fields. Fifteen nodes, the most-used foreground: on white it measures 4.6:1, which clears AA on this ground but would not on a tinted one — which is another reason the screen has exactly one surface.

The active step marker and the Publish affordance. A single appearance per screen state — the band is the only place the flow raises its voice, and it earns it by being the thing that gates completion.

n8.typography: System face throughout (-apple-system on the render), per the native DNA — a creation flow borrows the platform's own voice rather than announcing a brand mid-task. Four weights render: 300 for the step counter, 400 for field values and help, 600 for labels and the band's status sentence, 700 for step titles and the price figure. Scale measured at 390: 26px price figure, 22px step titles (six nodes — one per step plus the review summary), 20px section heads, 16px field values, 13px help text, 12px captions, 11px the step counter and unit suffixes, which carries twelve nodes and is therefore the tier that decides whether the form is scannable. Currency and figures use tabular alignment, but never in the same text node as the ₩ sign — RN Web renders that combination with a visible gap, a defect the previous round recorded.
n8.spacing: 4px is the base unit and the dominant gap (ten occurrences — label to field, icon to text, chip rows). 8px separates fields within a group, 12px separates groups, 16px sets the screen's horizontal inset, 20px and 24px handle the space above and below the fixed bands. The screen is three fixed regions and one scrolling one: a step tracker pinned to the top, a FlatList per step in the middle, and the action band pinned to the bottom. Each step renders exactly one list rather than nesting them — a category grid of eight and a condition list of five are laid out as wrapped rows inside a single list's sections, because nesting a FlatList inside a FlatList is the fastest way to break scroll behaviour on both platforms.
n8.philosophy:
The bottom band is a state machine, not a button. It never sits there as a dimmed Publish waiting for the form to be finished. Instead it names what is still missing — one sentence, in priority order when several things are — and pressing it jumps to the step that owns that gap. Publish appears only once nothing is left to say. That inverts the usual arrangement, where the control is present from the start and the user has to discover why it will not respond.

That pattern is not new here; it is the second round to use it. It was established one round earlier as a single checklist that scored inline checks, and this screen extends it across four ordered steps, which is what made it a reproduction rather than a variation. The canon now states the rule in the general form the two rounds share: a fixed bottom band is judged by whether it does work, not by whether it exists — say what is open, jump to it, and refuse to price a state that cannot be fixed.

Step transitions are announced rather than left to visual change: the band carries an alert role and the step tracker a polite live region, so the flow is followable without watching it.

dosDonts.do: Make the bottom band say what is still missing and jump to that step when pressed.
dosDonts.dont: Render a disabled Publish and let the user hunt for the reason. A dimmed control communicates that something is wrong, not what.

dosDonts.do: Announce step changes through an alert role and a polite live region.
dosDonts.dont: Rely on the tracker's visual state alone — the whole point of a wizard is that position is meaning.

dosDonts.do: Lay each step out as one list, with grouped rows inside it.
dosDonts.dont: Nest a FlatList inside a FlatList to fit a category grid and a condition list on the same step.

dosDonts.do: Keep one surface tone for every step.
dosDonts.dont: Tint steps to signal progress. The tracker already carries position, and a second signal for the same fact costs a colour you will want later.

dosDonts.do: Put the ₩ sign in its own text node beside the tabular figure.
dosDonts.dont: Combine them in one node — RN Web renders a visible gap between the sign and the digits when tabular-nums is applied.

dosDonts.do: Order the missing-field message by priority when several are open at once.
dosDonts.dont: List them all in the band. It is a sentence, not a validation summary; the summary belongs on the review step.

n8.agentPrompt:
Build a four-step seller wizard for a mobile marketplace: photos, category and condition, price, review and publish.

One surface only — white ground, near-black #18181b for titles and values, #52525b for explanations, #71717a for captions and the step counter, and a single accent #4f46e5 that appears on the active step marker and on the publish affordance. Nowhere else.

System face, four weights (300/400/600/700). Scale 26 / 22 / 20 / 16 / 13 / 12 / 11px, with 11px carrying the counters and unit suffixes.

Three fixed regions and one scrolling one: a step tracker pinned top, the step's content in the middle, an action band pinned bottom. Each step renders exactly one list — group rows inside it rather than nesting a second list.

The band is the design. It is not a disabled Publish. At any moment it states, in one sentence, what is still missing — priority-ordered when several things are — and pressing it moves to the step that owns that gap. Publish appears only when nothing is left to say. Give the band an alert role and the tracker a polite live region so the flow can be followed without watching it.

Spacing: 4px base, 8px within a group, 12px between groups, 16px screen inset, 20–24px around the fixed bands.

Currency: keep the ₩ sign in its own text node next to the tabular figure, never inside it.

Do not build this as a persistent list, a chronological thread, a checklist with a scoring band, or a single continuously-scrolling settings screen. Those screens exist.

palette.usage: The most-painted colour on the screen — eleven elements. The rail itself, the filled markers of completed steps, and the confirm band when it appears. Unusually heavy accent use for this catalogue, and it is doing structural work rather than decorative: the rail is the sequence.

Ground and the item summary and courier cards alike — nine elements. The cards are separated by border and elevation rather than by tone, which leaves the accent free to mean progress and nothing else.
The four step names and the item title. Six nodes — a deliberately small set, because on a timeline the reader's eye should land on position first and prose second.
Actual and estimated dates, the expanded detail line under each step. Eight nodes, the largest text tier — a status timeline is mostly dates, and this is the tone they are read in.
Section captions and the labels of steps not yet reached. Seven nodes. Pending steps are muted in tone as well as unfilled in marker, so the state reads without relying on the marker shape alone.
The single current step's title, one tick darker than the others. Three nodes — the only place the screen uses a fourth grey, and it exists because exactly one step is ever current.
The confirm band's label and the numerals inside filled markers. White on #4f46e5 measures 6.5:1 — comfortably above AA, which is what lets the band carry body-size text.

n9.typography: System face, three weights (400 for dates and detail, 600 for step titles and the band label, 700 for the order figure). Scale measured at 390: 28px order total, 17px item title, 16px step titles (nine nodes), 14px the band label, 13px dates and detail (nine nodes), 12px captions and status pills (eleven nodes — the largest tier), 11px the tracking-number monospace run. Dates use tabular figures so the actual and estimated columns align down the rail; the alignment is the reason a reader can tell at a glance which steps ran late without reading a single number.
n9.spacing: 8px and 12px carry the screen almost alone — 8px between a step marker and its label, 12px between rail segments, with 3px reserved for the tight gap between a date and its qualifier. 20px sets the vertical rhythm between cards, 16px the horizontal inset. The rail is a fixed-width column on the left with the step content flowing beside it, so a step's height is set by its own content and the rail stretches to match; that is what keeps a delivered step with three detail lines from breaking the rail's continuity. The confirm band is the only fixed chrome, and it is absent until it has something to do.
n9.philosophy:
The chrome appears only when it has work. While the reader is moving down four ordered steps there is no fixed band at all — the screen is a plain timeline. Once the order reaches Delivered, a Confirm receipt band takes the bottom of the screen. Before that point the same slot holds a banner naming the next step and its estimate instead, so the space is never a dimmed control waiting for permission.

That is the hypothesis this screen exists to hold. The catalogue already carries a screen with no fixed band at all and screens whose band is a state machine present from the start; this one proposes a third position — that the band's presence should itself be conditional on the state. It was not the round's winner. It was kept anyway, because dropping it would have left the open question about fixed bands with two positions and no artefact for the third.

Exactly one step is ever current, and step order is fixed rather than user-decided. That is what separates this from a checklist: the reader cannot reorder or skip, so the design owes them a clear answer to 'where is this now' before it owes them any controls at all.

dosDonts.do: Let the fixed band be absent until the state gives it something to do.
dosDonts.dont: Reserve the slot with a dimmed control. An empty band teaches the reader to ignore the bottom of the screen.

dosDonts.do: Fill the slot with a next-step banner and its estimate while the terminal action is unavailable.
dosDonts.dont: Leave the space blank — the reader's question before delivery is when, and the slot is where they will look for it.

dosDonts.do: Mark exactly one step as current, and mute the ones not yet reached.
dosDonts.dont: Let several steps read as active. A fixed sequence with two current positions is a checklist wearing a rail.

dosDonts.do: Use tabular figures for the actual and estimated dates so the columns align down the rail.
dosDonts.dont: Left-align mixed-width dates — the reader loses the ability to spot a late step without reading each one.

dosDonts.do: Let the rail carry the accent, since the sequence is the screen's structure.
dosDonts.dont: Spend the accent on the cards as well. Eleven painted elements is already a lot; spread it further and progress stops being the thing it signals.

dosDonts.do: Compute the current index and next step from the data.
dosDonts.dont: Hard-code the delivered state to make the band visible in a screenshot. The pre-delivery path has to exist in code even when the dummy data does not exercise it.

n9.agentPrompt:
Build a post-purchase order status screen for mobile: four ordered steps — payment confirmed, seller shipped, in transit, delivered — connected by a vertical rail.

White ground. #18181b for step titles, #27272a one tick darker for the single current step, #52525b for dates and detail, #71717a for captions and steps not yet reached. One accent, #4f46e5, and spend it on the rail and the completed markers — it is structure, not decoration. White on the accent (6.5:1) for the band label and marker numerals.

System face, three weights (400/600/700). Scale 28 / 17 / 16 / 14 / 13 / 12 / 11px. Tabular figures for dates, so actual and estimated align down the rail.

Spacing 8px marker-to-label, 12px between rail segments, 3px date-to-qualifier, 20px between cards, 16px inset. The rail is a fixed-width left column with content flowing beside it, stretching to match each step's own height.

The rule that matters: the fixed bottom band exists only when it has work. Before delivery the slot holds a banner naming the next step and its estimate. Once delivered, it becomes a Confirm receipt band. Never a dimmed control waiting for permission, and never blank.

Exactly one step is current; order is fixed and not user-decided. Compute the current index and the next step from the data rather than hard-coding a state — the pre-delivery path must exist even if your dummy order is already delivered.

Add an item summary card and a tap-to-reveal courier and tracking card. Do not build this as a chat thread, a togglable checklist, a settings list, or a filterable feed.
